abstract.p: The resilience and stability of industrial supply chains are the core pillars of the sustainable development of the global economy, and also an important foundation for achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals of “Responsible Consumption and Production” and “Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure”. To address the problem that traditional industrial supply chain risk assessment systems have fixed indicators and static weights, which are difficult to adapt to complex scenarios such as dynamic adjustments of supply chain nodes, fluctuations in market demand and changes in geopolitical patterns, and thus restrict the construction of sustainable supply chain resilience, this paper proposes a comprehensive indicator-weight dynamic evolution algorithm for industrial supply chain risk assessment systems. Firstly, the evolutionary characteristics and trigger rules of the industrial supply chain risk system are defined. Indicator-weight evolution is performed when the original indicator system can no longer meet the evaluation requirements. The Delphi method combined with the actual risk characteristics of the supply chain is adopted to determine the candidate indicator set. The candidate indicators are screened using the grey relational analysis algorithm and the entropy weight-variation coefficient method to construct the evolved risk indicator set. Secondly, an improved DEMATEL model is used to analyze the causal relationships among the evolved indicators. Evolutionary analysis of the original indicator weights is carried out according to the influence degrees between indicators, so as to obtain the evolved indicator weights and realize the dynamic linkage update of evaluation weights. This study conducts a case analysis using publicly available aggregated synthetic data on supply chain disruptions and resilience and compares the proposed method with the entropy weight–analytic hierarchy process (EW-AHP) and dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) methods. The performance of the methods is evaluated in terms of the consistency of indicator weights or relative importance, computational time, out-of-sample prediction performance, and retrospective analysis of a representative disruption event scenario. The results indicate that, under the current case and parameter settings, the proposed method can reconstruct the risk indicator system and coordinate indicator and weight updates, demonstrating certain advantages in computational efficiency and risk factor identification in the specified comparative experiments. It should be noted, however, that the current validation relies primarily on publicly available synthetic aggregated data and retrospective event-scenario analysis. Therefore, the evidence is insufficient to directly establish the risk-warning benefits or improvements in operational response efficiency that the method might deliver in real-world enterprise settings. This study provides a methodological framework for the coordinated updating of indicators and weights in dynamic industrial supply chain risk assessment. Its applicability across industries and practical effectiveness require further validation using independent data sources and actual enterprise operational data.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Industrial supply chain risk assessment systems serve as the core technical support for ensuring supply chain resilience and stability and achieving sustainable development of the industrial chain. The adaptability and scientific rationality of a system’s indicators and weights directly determine the effectiveness of assessment results, thereby affecting the long-term sustainable operation capacity of enterprises as well as the security and stability of supply chains. Traditional assessment systems use fixed indicators and static weights, which fail to meet the evaluation requirements of dynamic scenarios such as supply chain node adjustment, transportation mode changes, and policy iteration. This easily leads to deviations in risk assessment and does not easily satisfy the practical demands of full-life-cycle risk management and control for modern industrial supply chains [1]. Therefore, constructing an indicator-weight evolution system that can be dynamically adjusted along with the development of supply chains is of great theoretical value and practical significance for enhancing the risk resistance of industrial supply chains and ensuring the security and stability of industrial chains and supply chains.
Currently, domestic and foreign scholars have conducted extensive research on industrial supply chain risk assessment, forming a rich theoretical and methodological system.

In terms of supply chain risk assessment, Lyu J et al. [2] constructed a dynamic comprehensive evaluation model based on complex network theory to assess the importance of unexpected risks at global soybean supply chain network nodes, confirming the core positioning of key nodes through empirical analysis and the 2SLS method to address endogeneity. Dong et al. [3] integrated fuzzy logic and the entropy weight method to establish a risk assessment model for cross-border e-commerce logistics supply chains, realizing quantitative evaluation of multi-dimensional risks via a four-layer framework. Ampofoah et al. [4] explored the path of AI/ML models in generating supplier risk scores, verifying the superiority of text-enhanced models in risk prediction through case studies. Lyu C et al. [5] proposed a dual-objective optimization method combining Bayesian networks and information theory to solve the interruption risk management problem of multi-level supply networks under data scarcity. Xiang et al. [6] built a hybrid hesitant fuzzy DEMATEL-entropy weight coefficient of variation model to comprehensively evaluate low-carbon automotive supply chain risks and the correlation between factors.

The above studies have contributed to the improvement of supply chain risk assessment systems, but they have fundamental limitations in the aspect of dynamic evolution. Existing models generally adopt a preset static indicator system and one-time weight calculation mode. Whether it is the traditional entropy weight method, DEMATEL method or emerging machine learning models, none have established an active trigger mechanism based on environmental changes, and thus cannot update the risk indicator library in real time in response to external shocks such as geopolitical conflicts and policy adjustments. Meanwhile, these methods can only calculate static weights within a fixed indicator framework, ignoring the dynamic evolution of causal transmission relationships between indicators, and failing to realize the coordinated linkage between indicator addition/deletion and weight adjustment. This leads to problems such as incomplete coverage of risk factors, delayed weight updating and inaccurate evaluation results when facing rapidly changing situations.

Regarding the evolution of indicators and weights, MengLi et al. [7] coupled the ABCD hydrological model with deep learning algorithms to quantitatively assess the impact of human activities and climate change on hydrological drought evolution. ZhenCao et al. [8] used Sen’s slope trend test and interpretable machine learning models to reveal the spatiotemporal evolution rules and driving mechanisms of GPP, ET, and WUE in the Yellow River Basin. TingtingLiu [9] applied the entropy weight TOPSIS model combined with spatial analysis methods to realize dynamic measurement and regional difference analysis of food security levels in 30 provinces. MinhuaLu [10] constructed a multi-dimensional indicator framework and used the entropy method to reveal the evolutionary law of new quality productive forces driving sustainable development. ShuWang et al. [11], using a base DPSIR model combined with entropy weight TOPSIS and a Markov transition matrix, analyzed the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics and driving factors of tourism ecological security in the Silk Road Economic Belt.

It should be noted that the above evolutionary studies in hydrology, ecology, food security and other fields mainly focus on retrospective analysis of the spatiotemporal evolution laws of objective phenomena, aiming to reveal historical change trends and driving mechanisms. Their indicator systems are mostly pre-determined and relatively stable throughout the research period, and weight adjustments are usually performed periodically based on overall data characteristics rather than real-time response to sudden changes. These methods are suitable for characterizing the evolution of natural or socioeconomic systems with relatively slow rates of change. However, they cannot be directly applied to industrial supply chain risk assessment scenarios that require real-time dynamic sensing and rapid response capabilities, nor can they adequately address the rapid reconstruction of assessment systems in response to structural disruptions in supply chains.

Furthermore, recent studies have introduced optimal transport methods into supply chain structural analysis, providing a novel perspective on supply chain efficiency diagnosis. A geometric optimal transport-based analytical framework for sustainable closed-loop supply chains has been proposed, employing the Gromov–Wasserstein distance to jointly assess supply chain structure and attribute efficiency, thereby providing a quantitative tool for supply chain structural optimization [12]. While these studies focus on the static evaluation of supply chain structural efficiency, the present study investigates the dynamic evolution of risk assessment systems. Thus, the two approaches complement each other by advancing supply chain management methodologies from different perspectives.

In summary, numerous scholars have conducted extensive research on the management, diversification, and informatization of industrial supply chains. However, there are still significant shortcomings in the study of indicator-weight co-evolution models for complex scenarios, which are difficult to adapt to the dynamic evolution characteristics of industrial supply chains. This study focuses on addressing two key issues:

(1) How to construct a risk indicator set that dynamically adapts to changing supply chain conditions, enabling the proactive addition and removal of indicators and their dynamic adaptation to evolving risk profiles;
(2) How to establish a dynamic weight updating mechanism based on the interactions among indicators to realize the co-evolution of indicators and weights.

To address the aforementioned issues, this paper proposes an innovative comprehensive dynamic-evolution algorithm for the index-weight system of industrial supply chain risk assessment. Its core innovation lies in the construction of a complete two-stage “trigger-reconstruction” evolution framework, which breaks through the inherent limitation of traditional static assessment models—a fixed index set with one-time weight calculation. The specific contributions are outlined as follows:

(1) A quantitative dynamic evolution trigger mechanism is established. It realizes active perception of supply chain system changes, solving the problem that traditional static models fail to respond to external environmental shocks in real time.

(2) An index evolution screening method coupled with Delphi-GRA-entropy weight-coefficient of variation is constructed. From the dual dimensions of correlation and information contribution, it achieves dynamic addition and deletion of assessment indicators, ensuring that the index system can be dynamically adapted to changes in supply chain scenarios.

(3) The standard DEMATEL method is extended for dynamic index scenarios. A weight redistribution mechanism based on inter-index causal correlation degree is proposed, which realizes smooth linkage update of weights after index addition or deletion, and avoids the high cost of full-scale remodeling and recalculation in traditional methods.

Validated with independent samples across multiple industries, the evolutionary algorithm proposed in this paper exhibits strong generalizability and consistency. In contrast to most existing studies that focus on static weight calculation under a fixed index system, this paper forms a complete closed-loop dynamic assessment system covering trigger judgment, index reconstruction and weight updates, providing a new methodological approach for dynamic risk assessment of sustainable industrial supply chains.

sec.title: 2. Description of the Characteristics and Evolutionary Forms of the Industrial Supply Chain System
2.1. Characteristics of the Industrial Supply Chain System
sec.p: The primary task of industrial supply chain management is to construct a resilient supply chain system featuring end-to-end visibility, full-domain collaboration, and full-process controllability, in response to global market competition, industrial chain restructuring, and changes in the geopolitical landscape. It enables autonomous completion of various risk assessments and response decision-making, achieves high integration between the supply chain system and production and operation systems, and fully meets industrial production security requirements under a dynamic market environment. With the development of intelligence and flexibility in industrial manufacturing, the models and demands of industrial supply chains have also undergone corresponding changes. As the basis for subsequent risk control and optimization efforts, the industrial supply chain risk assessment system represents a critical link in supply chain resilience management.

Functionally, the industrial supply chain system is characterized by dynamic and variable task scenarios, continuously adjusted indicators, and a high degree of digital dependence [13]. In the actual operation of supply chains and risk control processes, with the replacement of core suppliers, adjustments to logistics and transportation routes, and constant changes in market demand, the evaluation indicators for industrial supply chain risk assessment are continuously evolving and updating, leading to certain complexity and fuzziness in their evaluation. Consequently, industrial supply chain risk assessment is inherently an evolutionary and dynamic process. As task scenarios change and supply chain entities are replaced, evaluation indicators are continuously added, deleted, or merged, with their weights changing accordingly.

sec.title: 2.2. The Triggering Mode of Industrial Supply Chain System Evolution
sec.p: The industrial supply chain system represents a state of system operation under the combined effect of changing demands and entities. During the development of the industrial supply chain system, it evolves accordingly with task shifts and market updates. Therefore, the evolution of the industrial supply chain system can be interpreted as major changes occurring in the supply chain over continuous time, leading to alterations in its overall structure, resource allocation, and evaluation indicators. As the supply chain system transitions from one operational state to another, the collaborative evolution of indicators and weights is triggered accordingly.
To quantify the evolution trigger rules, the following rules are proposed:

1. Benchmark Period: The period during which the supply chain system operates stably following the previous indicator-weight evolution. Each time a full evolution is accomplished, the benchmark period is updated to the first cycle of stable operation of the system after evolution.

2. Monitoring Window: This window is consistent with the minimum unit of the benchmark period. Only the average value of each indicator within the window is calculated to avoid triggering evolution due to accidental random fluctuations.
3. Trigger Cooling Period: The minimum evolution interval is set to two monitoring window cycles. Evolution will not be triggered within the cooling period even if the threshold is reached.

Based on the calculation rules set above, the abnormal change value is calculated every monitoring window period. When the overall abnormal change value of the supply chain is excessively large, collaborative evolution is triggered. The calculation formula of the abnormal change value is as follows:(1)δ=∑j=1mwjxj−x¯j02 where m denotes the number of monitoring indicators, wj represents the weight of the monitoring indicator, xj is the standardized value of the j-th indicator within the monitoring window, and x¯j is the standardized mean value of the j-th indicator during the benchmark period.

The threshold is set at 0.6. This value strictly follows the empirically validated general risk classification standard for industrial supply chain risk assessment [14]. Based on the retrospective analysis of more than 1200 typical supply chain disruption events worldwide and industry consensus, this standard divides the supply chain system risk level into three intervals with clear management implications: low risk (0–0.3); medium risk (0.3–0.6); and high risk (≥0.6).

Building on the aforementioned risk classification, this study further conducts a sensitivity analysis of five candidate thresholds: 0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65, and 0.70. This range was selected for the following reasons: thresholds below 0.50 may lead to normal local fluctuations being misclassified as systemic changes, whereas thresholds above 0.70 may delay responses to structural risks. Therefore, the range of 0.50–0.70 covers the primary decision-making spectrum from relatively sensitive to relatively conservative settings. The results indicate that a threshold of 0.60 provides a favorable balance among information retention, system redundancy, and risk response timeliness.

It should be noted that the threshold of 0.60 was not determined solely on the basis of the proposed method’s own composite score. Instead, it was further validated using external risk events independent of the threshold optimization process. Specifically, the 2024 Red Sea shipping disruption was selected as an external validation scenario, with the occurrence of the event and objective operational changes before and after the event serving as reference points. The results show that, at a threshold of 0.60, the model can identify a sustained increase in risk levels before the event occurs and trigger the coordinated evolution of indicators and their weights. Lower thresholds tend to increase false triggers during non-event periods, whereas higher thresholds may delay risk identification. Accordingly, 0.60 was ultimately selected as the evolution trigger threshold in this study. Empirical data from reference [14] shows that under the threshold of 0.6, the false trigger rate can be controlled within 8% and the missed trigger rate is less than 5%, which is the optimal value balancing assessment timeliness and system stability. Meanwhile, it is consistent with the critical values adopted in similar dynamic risk assessment studies by Guo et al. [14] and Lyu et al. [2], and has extensive academic consensus. The suitability of this threshold was further assessed through sensitivity analysis, with detailed results presented in Appendix A.

sec.title: 2.3. Overall Indicator-Weight Evolution Model for Industrial Supply Chain Risk Assessment
sec.p: This study designs a two-stage technical route of “trigger-reconfiguration” focusing on the dynamic evolution of indicators and weights in the industrial supply chain system, with the specific process as follows:

First, the system enters the trigger phase, calculates the abnormal value of the supply chain risk assessment system according to the rules, and enters the evolution phase when the abnormal value exceeds the threshold.

The system enters the indicator and weight evolution phase, which is divided into two modules: indicator evolution, and weight update. In the indicator reconstruction module, first, according to changes in the external environment and policy updates, the Delphi method is adopted to determine candidate indicators. It combines the original indicator system with candidate indicators to construct a new indicator system, and uses the Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) algorithm to complete indicator screening and realize indicator addition. The entropy weight-coefficient of variation method is used to couple the screening logic of important indicators to complete indicator deletion and finally form an evolutionary indicator system. In the weight update module, the improved DEMATEL model is used to conduct evolutionary analysis on the addition and deletion of weights. The causal relationships between indicators are obtained through the DEMATEL algorithm, and weight allocation is performed according to the comprehensive impact matrix.

Through the above phased and modular technical processes, the dynamic evolution of indicators and weights in the industrial supply chain system is realized, providing methodological support for the adaptive optimization of the system. sec.title: 3. Indicator Evolution Model for Industrial Supply Chain Risk Assessment System
sec.p: Indicator evolution serves as the prerequisite and foundation for updating the indicator weights in the industrial supply chain risk assessment system. To accurately evaluate the performance of the industrial supply chain risk assessment system under the constant changes in practical demands and supply chain entities, it is necessary to design corresponding models and algorithms to reconstruct the indicators. Specifically, models are constructed and restructured to accommodate the addition and deletion of indicators in the updated evaluation indicator set, enabling timely and accurate assessment of the supply chain risk system under dynamic scenarios. This provides a reference and guidance for subsequent risk judgment and precise management and control [15].

The composition of the risk evaluation indicator set changes dynamically with the evolution of the industrial supply chain system. Let the initial indicator system be Xe,0. Then, at the i-th moment, the supply chain risk assessment indicator set is expressed as:(2)Xe,i=a1,a2,⋯ai,⋯,an1≤i≤n
With the dynamic evolution of the industrial supply chain system, at the (i + 1)-th moment, the supply chain risk evaluation indicator set is:(3)Xe,i+1=a1′,a2′,⋯aj′,⋯,am′1≤j≤m

In the indicator evolution process, an expert panel is first established using the Delphi method to conduct analysis and multiple rounds of anonymous voting on changes in the external environment of the supply chain, policy adjustments, and other relevant factors, ultimately obtaining candidate indicators for potential addition to the system. The grey relational analysis (GRA) algorithm is then employed to perform grey relational screening on the candidate indicators, eliminating those with low correlation to supply chain risk assessment. Finally, indicators that pass the correlation test are incorporated into the original indicator system. Concurrently, the entropy weight-variation coefficient method is applied to remove redundant indicators with low comprehensive contribution from the indicator system, resulting in the final evolved evaluation indicator system.

sec.title: 3.1. Addition of Evaluation Indicators
sec.p: The Delphi Method is an expert collaborative decision-making approach based on multi-round anonymous consultation, feedback iteration and statistical aggregation, which can systematically integrate expert wisdom to form scientific and reliable decision conclusions [16]. The use of Delphi method in the dynamic evolution process of an industrial supply chain system can supplement the shortcomings of the original indicator system, adapt the systems to new supply chain environment and policy standards, and obtain the evaluation indicators that need to be added.

This study consulted five experts, including three academic researchers and two industry experts with experience in supply chain risk management in manufacturing enterprises. This expert panel provides professional judgment for the context-specific construction of the indicator system. However, the judgments obtained may be influenced by differences in individual professional backgrounds, industry experience, and risk perceptions. Therefore, expert opinions are used as a professional basis for candidate indicator identification and causal relationship analysis among indicators, rather than being treated as a statistical sample representative of the entire population of industrial supply chain experts. To examine the potential effects of variations in expert panel size on the analytical results, we conducted an exploratory sensitivity analysis using the existing five experts, comparing indicator evaluations and weight estimates across panels of three, four, and five experts. The purpose of this analysis is to identify potential differences arising from changes in the composition of the current expert panel, rather than to demonstrate the statistical stability or general applicability of the weight estimates across a larger expert population. Because all subsets were drawn from the same group of experts, the combinations do not constitute independent samples. Accordingly, the results should be interpreted cautiously in conjunction with the experts’ backgrounds, the characteristics of the indicator data, and the findings of other experiments. Future research should expand both the number and diversity of experts and incorporate a broader range of industry stakeholders to further examine the influence of expert judgments on indicator screening and weight estimation. The relevant results are presented in Appendix A. To ensure the scientific validity and practicality of the final evaluation indicator system, the following optimization criteria are set in this article:

(1) When experts have significant differences on the newly proposed indicators, the next round of discussion will be conducted to reevaluate them. The Kendall’s coefficient of concordance W is used to measure the consistency of expert ratings, and when W<0.6, indicating that expert opinions are not unified, the next round of consultation is required. The Kendall’s coefficient of concordance formula is:(4)W=12∑i=1mRi2−3n2mm+12n2mm2−12 where n is the number of risk indicators, m is the number of experts, and Ri is the sum of expert rating ranks for the i-th indicator.
(2) If a certain indicator shows high consistency and importance in multiple rounds of scoring, it will be retained in the final indicator system.
(3) If certain indicators are considered by most experts to have low correlation with supply chain risks or lack strong data, they will be deleted.

sec.title: 3.2. Deletion of Evaluation Indicators
sec.p: Based on the above analysis process, the list of newly added indicators Xe′,1 is obtained through the Delphi method. When the main tasks of the industrial supply chain change or entities are replaced, the indicator addition algorithm is used to update the original indicator system to make up for the shortcomings of the original indicator system in terms of insufficient environmental adaptability and coverage. Subsequently, the updated indicator system is screened and optimized by combining the GRA algorithm and the entropy weight-variation coefficient method to eliminate indicators with low correlation and redundant ones, thereby determining the final evaluation indicators to be added. The core idea of the GRA algorithm is to calculate the correlation degree between sequences by comparing the similarity of the curves of different sequences, to judge the correlation between the newly added indicators and the original indicator system and eliminate candidate indicators with low correlation. The entropy weight-variation coefficient method measures the information content of indicators according to the magnitude of their information entropy and the level of data fluctuation, which can effectively identify indicators with a high contribution rate in the industrial supply chain system and eliminate redundant indicators. Through the above two methods, the newly added evaluation indicators are deleted, screened and optimized from the perspectives of correlation and effectiveness, and finally the accurate evaluation indicators of the security system are obtained.

An indicator is defined as positive if its increase can reduce supply chain risk and improve supply chain stability; otherwise, it is defined as negative. According to grey systems theory, grey relational coefficients are commonly used within the range of 0.7–0.9 to distinguish moderate relationships from strong relationships. Accordingly, this study considered 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, and 0.90 as candidate thresholds rather than prespecifying 0.80 as the optimal value. In terms of threshold implications, values of 0.70 and 0.75 retain more candidate indicators but may introduce weakly related indicators into the evaluation system, thereby increasing indicator redundancy. In contrast, thresholds of 0.85 and 0.90 impose stricter screening criteria but may eliminate indicators with practical risk significance. Considering both indicator coverage and screening stability, a threshold of 0.80 represents a moderate choice. Furthermore, an independent risk event was used for external validation. Taking the 2024 Red Sea shipping disruption as a reference, this study compared the ability of indicators retained under different GRA thresholds to capture risk factors associated with the event. The results indicate that a threshold of 0.80 effectively retains risk factors directly related to the actual event, including geopolitical risks, cross-border logistics, and supply chain disruption response. Higher thresholds, by contrast, entail a greater risk of information loss. Therefore, 0.80 was ultimately selected as the grey relational screening threshold for newly added indicators.

This study examines the stability of the results around this threshold through one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity analysis and further validates its suitability using real-world risk events. Thresholds below this value tend to introduce redundant indicators, whereas higher thresholds may result in the loss of essential relational information. Detailed results are provided in Appendix A.
2. The specific steps of indicator screening using the entropy weight-variation coefficient method are as follows:
Step 1: Calculation of the information utility value of indicators using the entropy weight method.

The entropy weight method is an objective weight assignment method [18], which conducts correlation analysis on indicators by measuring the uncertainty and disorder of information. Based on the standardized original data of each indicator obtained from the above formula, the proportion Yij of the j-th sample value under the i-th indicator is calculated as follows:(10)Yij=yij∑i=1myij

The larger the utility value of an indicator, the more differentiated information it provides for different evaluation objects.

To address the issue of utility values approaching zero under extreme conditions, this study establishes a minimum utility threshold of 0.001. When an indicator’s utility value falls below 0.001, its information contribution is considered negligible, and the indicator is directly included in the candidate set for removal to avoid numerical instability caused by a near-zero numerator. Meanwhile, robustness tests conducted on all sample data show that the utility values of all indicators exceed the minimum threshold of 0.001, with no numerical instability observed. For example, indicator B13 has a utility value of 0.006, which exceeds the minimum threshold and falls within the model’s stable computational range.

Based on the information data of each indicator, the coefficient of variation method calculates the fluctuation degree of indicator data, which can objectively and effectively reflect the difference level among different indicators [19].

Then the normalized coefficient of variation w2i of the i-th indicator is given by:(15)w2i=vi∑i=1mvi where vi is the coefficient of variation, calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean value.
Step 3: Minimum information entropy coupling model.

Based on the principle of minimum information entropy, the indicator information obtained by the entropy weight-variation coefficient method is coupled [20], and the contribution rate of the new indicators to the entire indicator system is solved, to eliminate redundant indicators.(16)γi=w1i⋅w2i∑i=1mw1i⋅w2i where γi denotes the comprehensive contribution rate of the indicator. When an indicator exhibits a low utility value or coefficient of variation, it has insufficient information content and data variability. Such an indicator is considered redundant and unsuitable for weight allocation in the evaluation system. Therefore, it is excluded through the comprehensive contribution rate-based screening method.
Step 4: Screen indicators according to the comprehensive contribution rate.

Based on the comprehensive contribution rate, the indicators are sorted and summed in descending order of importance. In multi criteria screening, it is usually required that the cumulative information contribution rate reach over 90% to ensure the accuracy of the evaluation results, while avoiding the curse of dimensionality and increased computational complexity caused by too many criteria. To determine the optimal threshold, we analyze the marginal information increment under different cumulative contribution rates based on the data in Table 5. In terms of marginal information gain, increasing the cumulative contribution rate from 90% to 94% requires only two additional indicators and yields an effective information gain of approximately 4%. In contrast, increasing the cumulative contribution rate from 94% to 96% requires three additional indicators but yields only approximately 2% additional information, indicating a marked decline in the marginal information gain per indicator. Therefore, a threshold of 94% provides a favorable balance between information coverage and the number of indicators. To avoid determining the threshold solely on the basis of the composite score proposed in this study, external validation was further conducted using out-of-sample data and actual disruption events. Indicator systems constructed under different cumulative contribution rate thresholds were evaluated through out-of-sample risk prediction, using independent records of actual risk events and objective operational outcomes as benchmarks. The results indicate that a threshold of 94% maintains relatively high risk-information coverage while preventing excessive inclusion of low-contribution indicators. Both its out-of-sample predictive performance and its ability to identify core risk factors remain satisfactory. Accordingly, 94% was ultimately selected as the cumulative contribution rate screening threshold.

The optimality of this threshold was further assessed through sensitivity analysis. Deviations from this value may lead to increased system redundancy or insufficient information coverage. Detailed results are presented in Appendix A.

sec.title: 4. Weight Evolution and Reconstruction Model of the Industrial Supply Chain System
sec.p: The standard DEMATEL algorithm is a systematic factor analysis method based on graph theory and matrix operations. Its core function is to identify causal transmission relationships and key influencing factors among multiple factors in static systems, and it is widely applied in scenarios with fixed indicator systems and stable factor associations. However, when indicators in the assessment system change, this method cannot adapt to the core requirement of dynamic evolution of the indicator system with environmental changes in industrial supply chain risk assessment. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an improved DEMATEL weight reconstruction model which deeply integrates the core causal relationship identification capability of the standard DEMATEL with the dynamic weight update mechanism after indicator evolution. It not only clarifies the causal relationships among indicators, but more importantly, it constructs weight redistribution rules for indicator addition and deletion scenarios, realizing accurate and efficient evolutionary reconstruction of weights for industrial supply chain risk assessment. This provides a scientific reference for the overall risk optimization and improvement of supply chains in subsequent research. The core differences between the two are presented in Table 1 below:

Changes in the industrial supply chain evaluation indicator set will directly lead to the evolution of weights. However, due to the complex correlations among indicators, weights cannot be modified directly. The DEMATEL method can effectively handle the causal relationships and correlation calculations among multi-factor indicators, and is widely used in factor structure and causal relationship analysis [21]. Therefore, this paper adopts the improved DEMATEL model, fully considers indicator changes and internal correlations, and recalculates indicator weights based on the obtained comprehensive matrix to realize the dynamic evolution and evaluation of weights.

sec.title: 5.1. Problem Description
sec.p: Taking industrial supply chains as the research subject, this study evaluates and dynamically evolves the factors affecting supply chain stability. First, transportation and risk management data from a specific industrial supply chain are extracted for assessment and evolution analysis.

The data used in this paper are sourced from the Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Resilience database (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/bertnardomariouskono/global-supply-chain-disruption-and-resilience, accessed on 11 June 2026). Using the stratified random sampling method, a total of 10,000 complete supply chain records covering 2021 to 2024 are selected, involving six major trade routes (Asia-Europe, Trans-Pacific, Trans-Atlantic, Middle East-South Asia, Intra-Asia, and Africa-Europe) and 32 core ports, with a data completeness rate of 98.7%. To ensure sufficient statistical power for indicator screening and weight calculation, the original records are aggregated at a quarterly granularity (2021Q1–2024Q4, totaling 16 observations) based on the shipment date of each record. The number of records per quarter ranges from 582 to 674, with an average of 625, which fully captures the seasonal fluctuation characteristics of supply chain operations and satisfies the sample requirements of grey relational analysis and the entropy weight method.
The data preprocessing procedure consists of the following steps:

(1) Missing value imputation: Missing records, accounting for 1.3% of the dataset, were imputed using the three-year average for the same shipping route and corresponding period to ensure time-series completeness. For records with substantial missing data, estimates were made and supplemented based on the actual operational conditions of the enterprises.

(2) Outlier treatment: The 3σ rule was applied to identify and remove observations deviating from the mean by more than three standard deviations, thereby reducing the influence of extreme random events.

(3) Indicator aggregation: Each indicator was mapped to the corresponding raw data fields according to its function and definition. Indicator values were then calculated using the specified formulas, and the resulting raw indicator data were compiled. All indicators were aggregated into quarterly values according to the calculation rules specified in Appendix B.

To assess the robustness of the aggregation granularity, indicator values were also calculated at monthly and semi-annual intervals. The results showed a high degree of consistency in core indicator selection and weight rankings across the two alternative aggregation granularities, indicating that the main findings were not sensitive to the aggregation interval. Finally, the data were aggregated annually to obtain four sets of panel observations for subsequent indicator selection and weight calculation.

Drawing on previous studies [24,25], this study adopts 13 core indicators across four dimensions—operational and process adaptability, network structural resilience, external environmental shocks, and disruption and recovery capabilities—as the initial indicator set for industrial supply chain risk assessment. 5.2.1. Evaluation Indicator Addition
sec.p: 1. Selection of Candidate Indicators by Delphi Method

In strict accordance with the principles of authoritativeness, relevance, and representativeness for expert selection established in Section 2 of this paper, an expert advisory group of five members was formed. The experts are familiar with the practical impacts of the Red Sea shipping crisis and supply chain “de-risking” policies on the real industrial supply chain. With both theoretical depth and industrial practical experience, the expert team can accurately identify the core new risk dimensions of the current industrial supply chain, ensuring the scientific validity and practicability of the candidate indicator set.

First round of initial consultation: The original 13 core indicator system, basic data from the “Global Supply Chain Disruption and Resilience” database (2021–2024), and industry analysis reports on the 2024 Red Sea shipping crisis and supply chain “de-risking” policies of major economies were provided to the expert group. Through expert consultation, the core shortcomings of the original indicator system under the current situation changes were pointed out, and the risk indicators requiring addition were proposed.

Each expert scored the newly proposed indicators from three dimensions: relevance to overall supply chain risk, data availability, and current scenario adaptability. After this round of consultation, a total of eight preliminary candidate indicators were summarized, namely: C1 Geopolitical risk, C2 Extreme climate response rate, C3 Diversified cross-border logistics, C4 Supply chain warning response time, C5 Trade compliance risk level, C6 Concentration of supplier regions, C7 Exchange rate fluctuation risk, and C8 Proportion of carbon compliance cost. The scoring results are shown in Table 2 below:

The expert panel adopts a 1–5 scoring system, where 1 represents the lowest score and 5 represents the highest score. The corresponding semantic descriptions for scores 1 to 5 are: “Very low impact”, “Relatively low impact”, “Moderate impact”, “High impact”, and “Very high impact”, respectively. Relevant statistical indicators for each evaluation index, including the mean, standard deviation, rank, and correlation coefficients, are calculated based on the scoring sheets.

Second round of feedback and revision consultation: The mean, standard deviation, and rank statistics of the indicator scores from the first round were anonymously fed back to all experts. Experts were informed of the differences between their individual scores and the group mean, and supplementary industry background materials were provided for indicators with large discrepancies, asking experts to revise their scores. After this round of consultation, the Kendall’s coefficient of concordance was recalculated and obtained as W=0.69>0.6, indicating that expert opinions reached a high degree of consistency. Thus, the Delphi consultation was terminated.

Based on the results of the three rounds of consultation, indicators C7 and C8, whose average expert scores were less than 3 and with low recognition of risk correlation, were eliminated. Finally, six new core candidate indicators were determined, namely: C1 Geopolitical risk, C2 Extreme climate response rate, C3 Diversified cross-border logistics, C4 Supply chain warning response time, C5 Trade compliance risk level, and C6 Concentration of supplier regions.

sec.title: 5.4. Comparative Analysis of Methods
sec.p: This study compares the proposed indicator–weight evolution algorithm with two representative approaches. The first is the static entropy weight–analytic hierarchy process (EW-AHP), which represents a subjective–objective combined weighting method under a fixed indicator system. The second is the Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN), which represents a dynamic probabilistic model capable of capturing probabilistic dependencies among risk factors and their propagation over time. All three methods use the same 14 risk indicators derived from the final case study and follow consistent data preprocessing procedures and risk event labeling protocols to minimize the influence of differences in indicator inputs on the comparative results.

The comparison is conducted from four perspectives. First, the consistency and trend stability of the three algorithms are examined by analyzing the correlations between their indicator weights or relative importance scores. Second, the average computational time required to complete the entire modeling process is compared. Third, out-of-sample risk prediction errors and the hit rate for identifying the top five core risk factors are evaluated. Fourth, the 2024 Red Sea shipping disruption is used as an external validation scenario to compare changes in risk scores and the ability to identify key risk drivers. It should be noted that the direct output of a DBN is the posterior probability of a risk state rather than a conventional linear weight. To ensure comparability, the marginal effect of each indicator on the posterior probability of the high-risk state is used to represent its relative importance in the DBN. These importance scores are then normalized and compared with the weight vectors obtained from the other two methods.

Furthermore, the 16 quarterly observations obtained by aggregating the original data are not statistically equivalent to the underlying supply chain records. The former are used to characterize temporal variations at the quarterly level, whereas the latter are used to construct the corresponding indicator data. Since the estimation of conditional probability parameters in a DBN depends on valid time-series observations, the number of underlying records cannot be directly equated with the number of independent quarterly state-transition samples.

Given the limited number of quarterly time-series observations, the DBN training process preserves the chronological order of the data to avoid information leakage from the future that could result from randomly shuffling the time series. To mitigate parameter estimation instability under small-sample conditions, the network structure is constrained to avoid unnecessary parent-node connections, and state combinations occurring infrequently in the training data are handled explicitly. All preprocessing settings and model parameters are determined exclusively using the training data, while the test data are used only for out-of-sample evaluation.

To further avoid circular dependence between threshold selection and evaluation metrics, threshold validation is distinguished from the assessment of internal model performance. Sensitivity analysis is used to examine the effects of different thresholds on indicator retention, system redundancy, and weight stability. The final suitability of the selected thresholds is then evaluated using independent out-of-sample data and actual supply chain disruption events. External validation does not rely on the composite scores obtained from the threshold sensitivity analysis in this study; instead, it uses observed risk levels in out-of-sample data, the occurrence of actual disruption events, and objective operational changes as evaluation benchmarks.

sec.title: 5.4.1. Comparative Analysis of Consistency Among Different Methods
sec.p: This study adopts the Pearson correlation coefficient and Spearman rank correlation coefficient to compare the correlation of the two algorithms from the perspectives of numerical magnitude and ranking logic.

The specific procedures for analyzing and calculating risk factors and historical data via the entropy weight-AHP algorithm [27] are as follows: (1) Construction of the risk factor indicator system. To eliminate the impact of inconsistent indicator systems on the comparative results of the two methods, the final indicator system derived from the indicator evolution mentioned above is applied for evaluation. (2) Establish a judgment matrix through pairwise comparisons by experts, calculate eigenvectors to obtain the subjective weights of AHP, and conduct consistency tests. (3) Standardize the original data and compute the objective weights based on the entropy weight method. (4) Integrate subjective and objective weights using the linear weighting method.

The DBN algorithm [28] uses the 14 finalized risk indicators and the overall supply chain risk state as network nodes, with directed connections between adjacent time slices representing temporal dependencies in risk states. To control the number of parameters given the limited number of quarterly observations, the network structure is constrained based on expert knowledge and the causal relationships among indicators, avoiding unnecessary connections among all possible indicator combinations. DBN training consists of four steps: indicator state processing, network structure specification, conditional probability parameter estimation, and risk state inference. First, the discretization boundaries for each indicator are determined using the training samples, and continuous indicators are converted into a finite set of discrete states. These boundaries are determined exclusively from the training set and remain unchanged during testing. Second, the network structure is specified according to predefined causal relationships and temporal dependency rules, with the number of parent nodes for each node restricted to reduce the dimensionality of the conditional probability tables. Third, the conditional probability tables are estimated from state-transition frequencies in the training samples. Smoothing is applied to state combinations that are absent or infrequent in the training data to mitigate the zero-probability problem. Finally, given the current indicator states, the posterior probability that the supply chain is in a high-risk state is calculated. Because a DBN directly outputs the posterior probability of the supply chain entering a high-risk state rather than conventional linear weights, this study derives relative importance scores to facilitate comparison of the core risk factors identified by different methods. Specifically, the discrete state of each indicator is varied individually while all other conditions are held constant, and the resulting change in the posterior probability of the high-risk state is calculated. The absolute changes are then normalized to obtain the relative importance of each indicator.
The comprehensive indicator weights calculated using the EW-AHP and the DBN algorithms are presented in Figure 5.
Based on the weights of each indicator sent by three methods, a comparison chart of the weight distribution of each indicator is obtained, as shown in Figure 6.

The standard deviations and covariances of the weights assigned to the 14 indicators by the three algorithms were calculated and substituted into the corresponding correlation coefficient formulas. The resulting Pearson and Spearman rank correlation coefficients between the proposed evolution algorithm and the conventional entropy weight–analytic hierarchy process (EW-AHP) method were 0.917 and 0.943, respectively, indicating strong agreement between the two methods in assessing the relative importance of most core indicators. The Pearson and Spearman rank correlation coefficients between the proposed evolution algorithm and the dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) algorithm were 0.862 and 0.886, respectively. These differences may arise because the proposed method reconstructs the indicator set and adjusts indicator weights using DEMATEL, whereas the DBN primarily characterizes risk propagation through conditional probabilities and temporal dependencies. The above results indicate that, for the 14 risk indicators and the current data settings adopted in this study, the proposed evolutionary algorithm exhibits a high degree of numerical correlation and ranking consistency with the two benchmark methods in evaluating indicator importance. Furthermore, as illustrated by the indicator trend plots, the weight trends produced by the three algorithms are broadly consistent, suggesting that the proposed method demonstrates a certain degree of stability and credibility. However, given the limitations of the available data and validation scenarios, the applicability of these findings requires further examination using additional independent datasets and actual enterprise operational records.

sec.title: 5.4.2. Comparative Analysis of Computational Timeliness
sec.p: Industrial supply chain risk assessment requires not only accurate results but also timely updates in response to changing environmental conditions. Under identical hardware conditions (Intel Core i7-12700H processor and 16 GB RAM), the complete computational workflow of each of the three methods was executed 10 times, and the average runtime was calculated. To ensure consistency in the measurement scope, the runtime included model or indicator system construction, as well as one complete execution of weight updating or parameter learning and risk assessment. Non-computational activities, such as expert discussions and data downloads, were excluded. For the DBN, the first component included network structure initialization and conditional probability parameter learning, while the second comprised one round of risk state inference and indicator relative contribution calculation. The results are presented in Table 9.

The computational efficiency comparison reflects the time required by the three methods to complete one full evaluation workflow under the specific computational environment, data scale, and task definitions adopted in this study, rather than their general computational complexity across arbitrary data scales. To ensure a fair comparison, all three methods were evaluated using the same computational environment and timing rules, with the time required for model construction, weight calculation or parameter learning, and risk assessment measured consistently. Each method was executed 10 times, and the average runtime was used for comparison. The runtime of the DBN is closely related to its network structure, the number of states assigned to each node, the size of the conditional probability tables, and the parameter learning procedure. When the number of quarterly observations is limited, parameter learning itself may be relatively fast; however, the small sample size may also increase uncertainty in conditional probability estimation. Therefore, a shorter runtime does not necessarily imply higher predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency and predictive performance should be evaluated separately. The runtime comparison in this study is intended to characterize differences in computational costs among the three methods under the current experimental settings and should not, on its own, be used to infer their overall relative performance in real-world industrial supply chain environments.

The total runtime of the proposed evolutionary algorithm was 50.54 s, which was 27.38 s and 34.08 s shorter than those of the two conventional methods, respectively. This represents an improvement in computational efficiency of over 30%, demonstrating that the proposed algorithm can meet the requirements of rapid risk assessment in industrial supply chains. Although the proposed algorithm incorporates additional key steps, such as evolution trigger detection and indicator causal analysis, it substantially reduces computational time in two ways. During indicator system construction, only the existing indicator system needs to be updated in response to changes in the external environment, thereby saving considerable time. During weight calculation, weights are updated and adjusted based on the overall influence relationships among indicators, eliminating the need for computationally intensive weight-coupling calculations across multiple evaluation methods. Consequently, the proposed algorithm enables rapid reassessment of indicators and their weights in dynamic scenarios, significantly improving supply chain risk response efficiency.

sec.title: 5.4.3. Out-of-Sample Risk Testing
sec.p: To verify the practical risk assessment accuracy of the algorithm proposed in this paper, a time-series rolling out-of-sample test is designed. Different from in-sample weight correlation comparison, the out-of-sample test can directly reflect the method’s capability to identify unknown risks, and serves as a core indicator for measuring the practical value of dynamic assessment methods. The test scheme is designed as follows:

1. Training set: Based on sample data from Q1 2021 to Q4 2024 (a total of 16 quarterly observations), which is used to construct the indicator system and calculate initial weights for the two respective methods.
2. Test set: Data from Q1 to Q4 2025 are adopted as out-of-sample data to conduct supply chain sustainability assessment.

3. Reference benchmark: The actual comprehensive risk level, calculated based on the full sample and verified against the disruption events recorded in the dataset, is taken as the ground-truth risk benchmark.

Two metrics, namely the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of risk and the hit rate of Top-5 risk indicators, are selected as the criteria for comparison. The performance comparison results are presented in Figure 7 below:

As shown in this figure, the proposed evolutionary algorithm outperforms the conventional assessment methods on both out-of-sample evaluation metrics, nearly halving the risk score prediction error and substantially improving the accuracy of key factor identification.

In terms of methodological characteristics, EW-AHP relies on fixed weights that are less capable of adapting promptly to changes in risk drivers. DBN can model temporal dependencies and risk propagation, but its predictive performance is influenced by network structure, discretization methods, conditional probability estimation, and training sample size. In contrast, the proposed method responds to structural changes through trigger-based mechanisms, indicator screening, and coordinated weight updates.

sec.title: 5.4.4. Retrospective Validation Based on the Red Sea Shipping Disruption Event
sec.p: To further examine the dynamic response capability of the proposed algorithm to a typical supply chain disruption, this study selects the 2024 Red Sea shipping disruption as a case study and conducts a retrospective comparison of the risk assessment performance of different methods before and after the event, using event-related records from the publicly available *Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Resilience* dataset. The Red Sea shipping disruption was a real-world systemic risk event with a well-documented background and identifiable risk drivers, providing a real-event reference for comparing the responses of different risk assessment methods to major supply chain disruptions. It should be noted that the data used in this study consist of publicly available synthetic aggregated data rather than original operational records from a single enterprise. Accordingly, this section uses a real historical event as the analytical context for retrospective event-scenario validation. The primary objective is to examine the extent to which different methods capture changes in risk before and after the event and identify the key risk drivers. This validation provides supplementary evidence of the effectiveness of the proposed method under a typical disruption scenario. However, it cannot fully substitute for field validation using independent enterprise operational data. The applicability of the findings to enterprise-level risk early warning therefore requires further examination using actual operational data.

The test window is set from Q4 2023 (pre-event) to Q1 2024 (after the outbreak of the event). The risk identification performance of the two methods before and after the event is compared from two dimensions: the magnitude of change in comprehensive risk value, and the identification accuracy of core risk drivers. The comparison results are presented in Table 10.

The validation results demonstrate that the evolutionary algorithm proposed in this paper exhibits significantly stronger risk capture capability for real sudden disruption events. On the one hand, the evolutionary algorithm identified the rising trend of geopolitical and cross-border logistics risks as early as Q4 2023 and triggered the index-weight co-evolution mechanism, bringing the risk value close to the high-risk threshold before the outbreak of the event, which could provide enterprises with an early-warning window of approximately one quarter. In contrast, the static EW-AHP method did not exceed the high-risk threshold until Q1 2024, when the event had already exerted substantial impacts, showing obvious hysteresis in risk identification. DBN can capture certain temporal dependencies and risk propagation patterns; however, its adaptability to structural changes may still be constrained by fixed indicator inputs and network parameters. Given that this analysis uses quarterly observations and publicly available synthetic aggregated data, the risk increase observed one quarter before the event should be interpreted as a potential early-warning signal identified in this retrospective case study, rather than directly equated with a verified warning lead time in actual enterprise operations. Overall, the retrospective analysis of the Red Sea disruption provides supplementary evidence of the proposed method’s dynamic risk response capability in a typical disruption scenario, while also highlighting the need for further validation of its practical early-warning performance using independent enterprise operational data.

sec.title: 5.4.5. Cross-Industry Universality Verification
sec.p: To further verify the industrial applicability, conclusion robustness, and verification independence of the evolutionary algorithm proposed in this paper, and to address the limitation of insufficient single-scenario verification, the process-type chemical supply chain is selected as the independent verification subject. The data are sourced from the Wind Chemical Industry Chain Database and the Report on China’s Chemical Supply Chain Operation Index jointly published by the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing (CFLP). Samples are drawn from six leading listed chemical enterprises in China, covering 16 quarters of supply chain data spanning from Q1 2021 to Q4 2024. The number of valid observation samples per quarter ranges from 620 to 710, with an average of 665, which meets the statistical requirements of the algorithm proposed in this study. The data preprocessing procedure is consistent with that adopted in the original case.

Taking the stable operation period spanning Q1 2021 to Q4 2022 as the baseline period, the anomaly values are calculated in accordance with the evolutionary trigger rules specified in Section 2.2 of this study. Results indicate that, under the impacts of shocks including domestic pandemic lockdowns and surging international prices of chemical raw materials, the overall supply chain anomaly value reached 0.672 in Q2 2023. This figure exceeds the trigger threshold of 0.6, which satisfies the precondition for indicator-weight co-evolution. Drawing on the existing literature, an initial risk indicator system is constructed from four dimensions (Operational and Process Adaptability, Network Structure Resilience, External Environmental Shocks, and Disruption and Recovery Capability), encompassing a total of 12 core indicators. The specific indicators and their corresponding initial weights are presented in the Table 11 below.

Following the same expert selection criteria as the original case, a 5-member expert advisory panel was established. Through multiple rounds of Delphi consultations, six new candidate indicators are finally determined: Impact Coefficient of Epidemic Prevention and Control (C1), Raw Material Supply Guarantee Rate (C2), Main Line Logistics Smoothness (C3), Impact Degree of Environmental Production Restrictions (C4), Energy Cost Proportion (C5), and Supply Chain Digitalization Level (C6). The original indicators and candidate indicators are analyzed and processed in accordance with the indicator evolution method, and the evolved indicator system is obtained as follows.

In the first step, the GRA method is adopted, and eight quarters of supply chain data from 2021 Q1 to 2023 Q4 are selected as the benchmark. Taking the overall risk level of the chemical supply chain as the reference sequence, the correlation degrees of the six candidate indicators are calculated, and the processed raw data are presented in Appendix C. The average grey relational degree of each candidate indicator is derived according to the formula. The results show that the grey relational degrees of two indicators, namely the Impact Coefficient of Epidemic Prevention and Control and the Supply Chain Digitalization Level, fall below the threshold of 0.8 and thus are eliminated, while the remaining four candidate indicators with high correlation degrees are retained.

In the second step, the retained candidate indicators are incorporated into the initial indicator set, and the entropy-weight variation coefficient method is applied to calculate the comprehensive contribution rate of each indicator. Indicator screening is conducted based on the cumulative contribution rate, with the detailed calculation process provided in Appendix C. The calculation results indicate that the cumulative comprehensive contribution rate of the top 13 indicators reaches 94.4%, which satisfies the screening requirements. Three redundant indicators are eliminated from the candidate indicators, including Production Safety Risk and Average Recovery Time from Unit Failure from the initial indicators, and Impact Degree of Environmental Production Restrictions. Finally, a chemical supply chain risk indicator system consisting of 13 core indicators is formed through evolution.

Using the improved DEMATEL model proposed in Section 4 of this paper, causal correlation analysis and weight update calculations are performed on the evolved indicator system. The expert scoring table and DEMATEL calculation results are presented in Appendix C. The results of indicator causal classification show that six indicators, including raw material price volatility, diversification of raw material transportation routes, and core supplier concentration, are cause indicators, which serve as the core driving factors of chemical supply chain risks; six indicators, including on-time delivery rate and production unit utilization rate, are effect indicators and represent the terminal manifestations of supply chain risks.

Two indicators, B7 and B11, are eliminated from the initial 12 indicators. Based on the comprehensive influence matrix, the set of indicators that have significant correlation with the deleted indicators is identified, and weight incremental adjustment is carried out to avoid weight distortion caused by direct deletion. The newly added indicators C2, C3 and C5 are incorporated into the DEMATEL evaluation system. Supplementary expert scoring is conducted for the impact relationships between the newly added indicators and the original 10 indicators, and the comprehensive influence matrix and the importance degree of each indicator are recalculated.
