The weight evolution results yield three main findings. First, the three newly added indicators, including Raw Material Supply Guarantee Rate, Main Line Logistics Smoothness and Energy Cost Proportion, all rank among the top in terms of weight. They accurately reflect the shift in core risks in the chemical supply chain from the production side to the supply and logistics sides under the shocks of pandemic lockdowns and raw material price hikes, which is highly aligned with the industry’s actual risk priorities. Second, cause indicators have a larger overall weight adjustment amplitude than effect indicators. This conforms to the design logic of the improved DEMATEL model proposed in this study that weights dynamically interact with causal transmission relationships, and verifies the rationality of the weight redistribution mechanism. Third, cross-scenario comparison shows that both industries follow the same pattern after evolution. The weights of external shock indicators rise, while those of conventional operation indicators decline relatively. Meanwhile, On-time Delivery Rate remains the core effect indicator throughout the analysis, which confirms the cross-industry consistency of the method’s evolutionary logic.

Unlike the retrospective scenario analysis of the Red Sea shipping disruption presented in Section 5.4.4, this section uses supply chain data from the chemical industry obtained from a different source to examine the applicability of the proposed method in another industrial sector. Provided that these data were not used in model construction or parameter calibration, this cross-industry analysis offers additional evidence of the method’s applicability from the perspectives of both data provenance and application context.

sec.title: 5.4.6. Results and Discussion
sec.p: Taken together, the above validation results demonstrate that the proposed indicator–weight co-evolution algorithm offers substantial performance advantages in dynamic scenarios. These improvements primarily stem from three design features. First, the trigger mechanism enables proactive updates to the assessment framework, mitigating the lag inherent in static models following environmental changes. Second, indicator evolution incorporates both correlation and information contribution to screen indicators, ensuring that the indicator system remains appropriate for the evolving scenario. Third, the improved DEMATEL-based weight redistribution mechanism leverages causal transmission relationships among indicators to achieve incremental and smooth weight updates.

Compared with existing studies, our findings are consistent with those of Lyu et al. [2], who identified policy factors as key drivers of supply chain risk, with both studies confirming the systemic influence of external environmental variables on supply chain systems. However, this study further quantifies the propagation effects of weight changes following indicator addition or removal and reveals risk transmission pathways associated with indicators such as production capacity flexibility, thereby addressing a gap in existing research on dynamic weight updating mechanisms. Compared with the hybrid fuzzy DEMATEL model proposed by Xiang et al. [6], the key advantage of our method is its ability to accommodate dynamic changes in the indicator set, rather than calculating weights solely within a fixed indicator framework. This makes it better suited to scenarios involving structural changes, such as geopolitical conflicts and policy adjustments.

Nevertheless, the proposed method has certain applicability boundaries. In stable systems where the indicator framework does not require adjustment, its performance advantage over conventional static methods is limited, while its computational complexity is slightly higher. The benefits of the proposed method become more pronounced only when structural changes occur and the existing indicator system becomes less suitable for the evolving environment.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: This study addresses three major limitations of conventional industrial supply chain risk assessment systems: fixed indicator sets, static weights, and limited adaptability to dynamic conditions. To overcome these limitations, we propose an innovative two-stage integrated algorithm for indicator–weight co-evolution based on a “trigger–reconstruction” mechanism. By integrating indicator evolution and weight evolution, the proposed algorithm enables dynamic updates to the assessment framework. Validation across multiple scenarios demonstrates strong internal consistency: the Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients between the weights generated by the proposed algorithm and those obtained using the conventional EW-AHP and Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) methods both exceed 0.8, while computational efficiency is substantially improved. External validation further demonstrates the practical advantages of the proposed algorithm: out-of-sample risk prediction errors are reduced by more than 40%, and risk identification for disruption events in the test set occurs approximately one quarter earlier than with static methods. These results indicate that the proposed algorithm enhances dynamic risk responsiveness. However, the above results are limited to the data, parameter settings, and evaluation tasks used in this study. Correlations between different weighting methods reflect the degree of consistency among the methods, while the retrospective analysis of the Red Sea shipping disruption based on publicly available synthetic aggregated data constitutes event-scenario validation and cannot substitute for independent external validation. Furthermore, the practical effects of the proposed algorithm on risk losses, warning lead times, and operational response efficiency have not yet been verified using actual enterprise operational data or real-world deployment trials. Therefore, the primary contribution of this study is to propose and preliminarily evaluate a dynamic indicator–weight co-evolution mechanism, rather than to claim that it has already been proven to deliver definite practical benefits across all industrial supply chain settings. Future research will use multiple independent data sources, actual enterprise operational records, and long-term follow-up trials to further evaluate the predictive validity, scope of applicability, and practical managerial value of the proposed method.

In terms of theoretical contributions, this study establishes an indicator–weight co-evolution framework for industrial supply chain risk assessment, moving beyond conventional static-assessment approaches and enriching the theoretical foundation of sustainable supply chain risk management. In practical terms, it provides a standardized dynamic assessment procedure that can serve as a methodological reference for the routine supply chain risk management of industrial enterprises engaged in cross-border trade. From a managerial perspective, the proposed framework establishes a quantitative evolution trigger mechanism, specifying that system updates should be initiated when the overall supply chain deviation value reaches or exceeds 0.6. This mechanism balances assessment timeliness with system stability and provides a scientific basis for long-term sustainable development planning. The results demonstrate that, within the scenarios tested in this study, the proposed algorithm can rapidly update industrial supply chain risk indicator weights, better align the assessment framework with dynamic supply chain characteristics, and substantially improve the timeliness and accuracy of risk assessment.

sec.title: 6.1. Limitation Analysis
sec.p:
Although the evolutionary algorithm proposed in this paper has achieved good results in industrial supply chain risk assessment, this study still has the following limitations:
Limited industry applicability: The evolutionary algorithm proposed in this paper is primarily constructed around general discrete manufacturing industrial supply chains, and the case validation is conducted with cross-border trade industrial supply chains as the research object. It has not yet been verified for adaptability in segmented fields such as process industries and military special industries, and the generalizability of the algorithm across different industries remains to be further examined.
Subjective bias in expert evaluation: The Delphi method involved five experts, which may not adequately capture differences in professional backgrounds, industry types, and risk perceptions, potentially introducing selection and group cognitive biases. Although Kendall’s W was used to assess agreement, the small sample limits statistical inference and representativeness. High agreement therefore does not constitute sufficient statistical validation of the indicator selection results. The expert-number sensitivity analysis assesses model stability within the existing sample range but cannot replace independent validation with a larger expert panel.
Single data source: The case study solely relies on historical panel data from the single database of “Global Supply Chain Disruptions and Resilience”, without integrating multi-source heterogeneous information such as internal enterprise operation data, real-time industry monitoring data, and policy text data. The aggregated nature of the dataset means that the validation of real-world disruption events is scenario-based and retrospective. The applicability of the findings at the enterprise level requires further validation using actual operational data.
Unverified long-term effectiveness: This paper only completed a single case validation of indicator-weight evolution based on historical panel data. It has not verified the stability of the algorithm in multi-round continuous evolution scenarios through long-term operation tracking data of industrial enterprises, nor has it conducted a systematic multi-dimensional comparative analysis with mainstream dynamic assessment models.

sec.title: 6.2. Future Improvement Direction
sec.p:
In view of the above limitations, further research can be carried out in the following aspects:
Development of industry-differentiated tools: Targeting the characteristics of process industries (continuous production, high process rigidity, and wide impact scope of accidents) and the features of military special industrial supply chains (high closure and strict confidentiality requirements), we will differentially adjust evolutionary trigger thresholds, indicator screening weight benchmarks and causal association calculation rules to construct a dedicated evolutionary algorithm system for different industries. Meanwhile, combined with tools such as Python (version 3.9) and MATLAB (R2021a), we will develop and integrate core modules including indicator evolution, weight reconstruction, result visualization and risk early warning, so as to expand the application scope and industry generalizability of the algorithm.
Multi-data source fusion verification: A multi-source heterogeneous data system integrating industry statistical data, enterprise ERP system data, real-time monitoring data from IoT devices and policy and public opinion text data will be constructed to solve the one-sidedness problem of single data sources.
Subjective and objective bias suppression methods: The Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (FAHP) and machine learning-assisted scoring mechanism will be introduced to design differentiated quantitative mapping models for different types of qualitative indicators. The sample size of Delphi experts will be expanded to 10–15, covering multiple entities including academia, industry and regulatory authorities, to further reduce the influence of subjective factors on assessment results.
Long-term effectiveness verification: Long-term cooperation will be established with 3–5 large industrial enterprises from different industries to collect real operational time-series data of more than 3 years, and carry out multi-round continuous evolution verification to evaluate the stability, robustness and cumulative error control capability of the algorithm in long-term dynamic scenarios. From the three core dimensions of assessment accuracy, computational efficiency and risk response speed, we will conduct a systematic comparison with mainstream methods such as dynamic Bayesian network models, LSTM time-series risk prediction models and reinforcement learning dynamic assessment models to quantify the relative advantages and applicable boundaries of the proposed algorithm.

app.title: Appendix A
app.p: To examine the reasonable ranges of the three core thresholds, a one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity analysis was first conducted using a controlled-variable approach. For each threshold, five levels were selected within theoretically and empirically supported ranges, with only one threshold varied at a time while all other parameters remained constant.

The evolution trigger threshold was set to 0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65, and 0.70; the grey relational screening threshold was set to 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, and 0.90; and the cumulative contribution rate was set to 90%, 92%, 94%, 96%, and 98%. These ranges cover the main levels of sensitivity, moderation, and conservatism.

The sensitivity analysis focused on three indicators: information retention rate, system redundancy, and result deviation. The information retention rate reflects the information coverage of the indicator system, system redundancy measures its compactness, and result deviation captures the effect of threshold variations on the stability of the weighting results. This analysis was intended solely to identify patterns in the model’s internal responses to different threshold settings; the composite score proposed in this study was not used as the sole basis for final threshold selection.

A linear weighted-sum method was used to aggregate the three dimensions, with weights of 40% for information retention rate, 35% for system redundancy, and 25% for result deviation. Higher scores indicate greater overall suitability of the threshold values. The threshold ranges were selected in accordance with commonly used practices in supply chain risk assessment and multi-criteria decision-making.

app.p: The validation process does not use the composite score jointly calculated from the three thresholds proposed in this study as the “ground truth,” thereby reducing circular dependence between threshold selection and validation metrics. Based on the combined results of the sensitivity analysis and external validation, the final thresholds were set to 0.60 for the evolution trigger, 0.80 for grey relational screening, and 94% for the cumulative contribution rate. These thresholds were selected according to three main principles: 0.60 balances false and missed triggers; 0.80 balances candidate indicator coverage and redundancy control; and 94% balances information coverage and the number of indicators. External validation further indicates that this threshold combination can effectively identify changes in actual supply chain risks, supporting its practical applicability.

To examine the influence of expert sample composition on indicator-weight calculations, the results obtained using all five experts with equal weights were taken as the baseline. Scenarios involving three, four, and five experts were then constructed. For the three-expert scenario, all 10 possible expert combinations were enumerated; for the four-expert scenario, all five possible combinations were examined; and for the five-expert scenario, the complete expert panel was used. Expert ratings within each subset were aggregated with equal weights, and indicator weights were recalculated using the same DEMATEL procedure.

Sensitivity was assessed using four metrics. First, Kendall’s W was calculated for each expert subset to evaluate the level of agreement among experts under different sample sizes. Second, the Pearson correlation coefficient between each subset’s weight vector and the baseline weight vector derived from all five experts was calculated. Third, the overlap ratio of the five highest-weighted indicators was measured. Fourth, the mean absolute change in indicator weights relative to the baseline was calculated. app.p: Table A4 compares indicator evaluation and weight calculation results obtained using different numbers of experts and different expert subsets selected from the five experts currently involved in the study. This analysis examines whether variations in the number of experts lead to substantial differences in the results within the scope of the current expert sample. Because the subsets share some experts, the results do not constitute mutually independent repeated trials. Furthermore, the results obtained from three- or four-expert subsets cannot be considered representative of resampling from a broader expert population. Therefore, even if certain indicators maintain similar rankings across different expert combinations, this can only suggest a degree of consistency within the current expert sample and does not establish that their weights have been sufficiently validated. For indicators exhibiting substantial variation across expert combinations, the potential sensitivity of their results to expert judgments is acknowledged in the discussion. Future research should further investigate the influence of expert judgments on the indicator system and weighting results by expanding the expert sample, increasing the diversity of industrial and professional backgrounds, and incorporating independent enterprise data for additional validation.
